q: Plato's version of this idea says that the world we perceive is a copy of perfect, unchanging entities such as Beauty, Justice, and the Good. Objects in the physical world "participate" in these entities. Aristotle criticized this view, saying that they should be in things themselves. For 10 points, name this theory about a realm of abstract ideals.

Gorgias, Hippias, and Prodicus were members of this group of itinerant teachers in fifth-century Greece. They charged fees to teach rhetoric and skills for success in the city. Socrates criticized them for valuing persuasion over truth. For 10 points, name this group whose name is now used for people who use clever but misleading arguments.

This Greek term for the highest human good is often translated as "flourishing" or "happiness." Aristotle held that it consists of virtuous activity of the soul. Its name literally refers to having a good guiding spirit. For 10 points, give this Greek word that is central to the ethics of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.

The Roman emperor Justinian is traditionally said to have closed this institution in 529 AD, ending nearly a millennium of philosophy there. It was founded near a grove named for the hero Akademos. Its later heads included Arcesilaus and Carneades, who adopted a skeptical outlook. For 10 points, name this school that took its name from the Athenian grove where Plato taught.
Answer these questions about Socrates.
parts: The Socratic method proceeds by asking probing questions to expose contradictions. Its Greek name for this refutation is the elenchus. Socrates was condemned in what city?
What comic playwright mocked Socrates as a cloud-worshipping sophist in a play of 423 BC?
Which handsome Athenian general was a companion of Socrates and later defected to Sparta?

q: Answer these questions about Aristotle's metaphysics.
parts: What term names the first cause, which moves everything else without itself being moved?
What term names his view that every physical object is a compound of matter and form?
What Greek term names the full realization of a thing's potential, such as an acorn becoming an oak?

q: Answer these questions about dialogues of Plato.
parts: Which dialogue, set at a drinking party, has speakers praising Eros, or love?
In which dialogue does Socrates guide a slave boy to double the area of a square, to argue that learning is recollection?
Which late dialogue, which includes the story of Atlantis, describes a craftsman called the Demiurge?

q: Answer these questions about Greek philosophical terms.
parts: What Greek word meaning "word" or "reason" names the rational order of the universe in Stoic thought?
What Greek word means "end" or "purpose," and underlies Aristotle's teleology?
What Greek word, used by Aristotle and Plato, refers to the soul?

q: Answer these questions about the Republic.
parts: In Book I, which sophist claims that justice is nothing but the interest of the stronger?
In Book II, Glaucon tells of a shepherd who finds a ring that makes him invisible. Whose ring is it?
The dialogue closes with a myth about a soldier who returns from death to tell what he saw. Which soldier?

q: Answer these questions about Pythagoras.
parts: Pythagoras founded his community in Croton. In which modern country is Croton located?
He is credited with the idea that the planets produce a harmony as they move. What phrase names this idea?
Pythagoreans revered a triangular arrangement of ten dots in four rows. What is this symbol called?

q: Answer these questions about Hypatia.
parts: Hypatia taught philosophy and mathematics in which Egyptian city?
Hypatia was a leading teacher in which Platonic school of late antiquity, which centered on Plotinus's ideas?
Hypatia was a woman philosopher and mathematician who died in what century AD?

q: Answer these questions about the Hellenistic and Chinese schools.
parts: Which school took its name from the porch in Athens where Zeno of Citium taught?
Which Chinese school, associated with Han Feizi, held that strict laws and punishments are the basis of order?
Which Chinese thinker taught "impartial care" and opposed Confucian ritual?

q: This thinker imagined a malicious demon who deceives him about everything. In Meditations on First Philosophy, he decides that the one thing he cannot doubt is his own existence as a thinking thing. He also invented analytic geometry, in which Cartesian coordinates are used. For 10 points, name this French philosopher who said "I think, therefore I am."

This philosopher argued that the mind begins as a blank slate, a "tabula rasa," and that all ideas come from experience. His Essay Concerning Human Understanding is a foundational text of empiricism. In his Two Treatises of Government, he argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property. For 10 points, name this English philosopher.

This Scottish philosopher's Treatise of Human Nature argued that the self is nothing but a bundle of perceptions. He raised the problem of induction and the claim that one cannot derive an "ought" from an "is." Immanuel Kant said this thinker's work awakened him from his "dogmatic slumber." For 10 points, name this author of An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding.

This philosopher from Konigsberg wrote that he was awakened from his "dogmatic slumber" by Hume. He distinguished between the phenomenal world of appearances and the noumenal world of things in themselves. He formulated a moral law that tells us to act only on principles we could will to be universal. For 10 points, name this author of the Critique of Pure Reason.

In Leviathan, this English philosopher argued that life in the state of nature would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." He said that people escape the war of all against all by surrendering their rights to an absolute sovereign. His book takes its name from a biblical sea monster. For 10 points, name this author of a work on political authority.

This Genevan philosopher began a book with the line "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." He argued that legitimate government rests on the general will and wrote the novel-treatise Emile on education. He also wrote an autobiography titled Confessions. For 10 points, name this author of The Social Contract.

This Victorian philosopher defended individual freedom in On Liberty and argued for the harm principle. He was educated rigorously by his father James and wrote The Subjection of Women. He refined an ethical theory by saying it is "better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied." For 10 points, name this British utilitarian thinker.

This English philosopher proposed the "felicific calculus" to measure pleasure and pain. He designed a circular prison called the Panopticon, in which a single guard could observe all inmates. His preserved body, called the Auto-Icon, is displayed at University College London. For 10 points, name this founder of modern utilitarianism.

This German philosopher wrote Thus Spoke Zarathustra and proclaimed that "God is dead." He introduced the idea of the Ubermensch and the thought experiment of eternal recurrence. His On the Genealogy of Morality contrasts master and slave morality. For 10 points, name this author of Beyond Good and Evil.

This Danish thinker wrote Fear and Trembling under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio. In it, he discusses Abraham's willingness to sacrifice Isaac as a "teleological suspension of the ethical." He broke off an engagement to Regine Olsen. For 10 points, name this author of Either/Or, often called the father of existentialism.

This philosopher's Phenomenology of Spirit appeared in 1807, and his Philosophy of Right claims that "the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk." He described history as the unfolding of freedom through a dialectical process. He taught at the University of Berlin. For 10 points, name this German idealist.

This philosopher's The World as Will and Representation argued that the world's inner essence is a blind, striving will. He taught that life is suffering and that relief comes from art and compassion. He was strongly influenced by the Upanishads and scheduled lectures at the same time as his rival Hegel in Berlin. For 10 points, name this German pessimist.

This philosopher's Ethics was written in the style of Euclid's geometry, with definitions, axioms, and propositions. He identified God with Nature in the phrase "Deus sive Natura" and held that only one substance exists. He was expelled from the Amsterdam Jewish community in 1656 and earned a living grinding lenses. For 10 points, name this Dutch rationalist.

This German philosopher believed that the universe consists of simple, indivisible substances called monads. He argued that this is "the best of all possible worlds" in his Theodicy. He also independently developed calculus alongside Newton. For 10 points, name this rationalist who proposed pre-established harmony.

This Irish bishop argued that "to be is to be perceived" and denied the existence of material substance. His Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous defend his idealism against skepticism. A California city and its university are named for him. For 10 points, name this empiricist who wrote A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge.

This German thinker wrote Das Kapital and, with Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto. He developed historical materialism, which holds that economic conditions shape society. He ended the Manifesto with "Workers of the world, unite!" For 10 points, name this author who analyzed class struggle between bourgeoisie and proletariat.

This Austrian-born philosopher wrote the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, which ends: "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent." His later work, published after his death as Philosophical Investigations, introduces language games and a private language argument. He taught at Cambridge. For 10 points, name this philosopher of language.

This British philosopher wrote Principia Mathematica with Alfred North Whitehead. He discovered a paradox about the set of all sets that do not contain themselves, and his "theory of descriptions" appeared in "On Denoting." He received the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature. For 10 points, name this author of Why I Am Not a Christian.

This English statesman wrote the Novum Organum, which urged scientists to base conclusions on systematic observation and induction. He warned about "idols" that distort the mind and is credited with the phrase "knowledge is power." He served as Lord Chancellor under James I. For 10 points, name this author of New Atlantis.

This Florentine wrote that it is safer for a ruler to be feared than loved, if he cannot be both. His most famous book, dedicated to a member of the Medici family, discusses virtu and fortuna. He also wrote Discourses on Livy. For 10 points, name this author of The Prince.

This French Enlightenment writer satirized Leibnizian optimism in Candide. He wrote the Treatise on Tolerance after the Calas affair and used the slogan "crush the infamous thing" against religious fanaticism. He had a long relationship with Emilie du Chatelet. For 10 points, name this French author who used a pen name instead of his birth name, Francois-Marie Arouet.

This French thinker argued in The Spirit of the Laws that power should be divided among branches of government so that one power checks another. His ideas about separation of powers strongly influenced the framers of the United States Constitution. He also wrote the epistolary satire Persian Letters. For 10 points, name this Baron de La Brede.

This English writer's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman argued that women should be educated alongside men. Her earlier work, A Vindication of the Rights of Men, responded to Edmund Burke. She died shortly after giving birth to the author of Frankenstein. For 10 points, name this early feminist philosopher.

This Irish-born statesman wrote Reflections on the Revolution in France, warning that radical change would lead to chaos. He also wrote a treatise on the sublime and the beautiful. He is considered a founder of modern conservatism. For 10 points, name this British politician and thinker who defended tradition and prescription.

This Scottish philosopher's The Wealth of Nations describes how a pin factory shows the benefits of division of labor. He used the image of an "invisible hand" to explain how self-interested actions can benefit society. An earlier book, The Theory of Moral Sentiments, emphasizes sympathy. For 10 points, name this founder of classical economics.

This author spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a poll tax, an experience that led to his essay "Civil Disobedience." He lived for two years in a cabin near a pond in Concord, Massachusetts. He described the experience in a book subtitled Life in the Woods. For 10 points, name this transcendentalist author of Walden.

This Concord-based essayist wrote "Self-Reliance" and "The American Scholar," the latter called America's intellectual declaration of independence. His book Nature helped found the movement of transcendentalism. He mentored Henry David Thoreau. For 10 points, name this American writer who urged "trust thyself."

This French philosopher coined the word "sociology" and proposed the law of three stages: theological, metaphysical, and positive. His Course of Positive Philosophy argued that knowledge should be based on observation. He designed a "religion of humanity" in his later years. For 10 points, name this founder of positivism.

This English-born pamphleteer wrote Common Sense in 1776, urging American independence. He later wrote Rights of Man in defense of the French Revolution and The Age of Reason, which criticized organized religion. His series The American Crisis begins "These are the times that try men's souls." For 10 points, name this author.

This French writer edited a landmark multivolume reference work with Jean le Rond d'Alembert. He also wrote the dialogue Rameau's Nephew and the novel Jacques the Fatalist. He was a leading materialist of the Enlightenment. For 10 points, name this editor of the Encyclopedie.
Answer these questions about Locke's major works and ideas.
parts: Which work of 1689 argued that governments exist by the consent of the governed and may be overthrown if they violate natural rights?
Which 1689 work argues that the mind begins as a blank slate?
Locke distinguished qualities such as shape and motion from qualities such as color and taste. What term names the first kind, which he believed exist in objects themselves?

q: Answer these questions about Kant's critical works.
parts: Which 1781 book asks what we can know about reality and argues that experience is shaped by categories of the mind?
What is the name for Kant's central moral principle, which says to act only on rules you could will as universal laws?
Which Kant book of 1790 discusses the beautiful and the sublime?

q: Answer these questions about Nietzsche's ideas.
parts: Nietzsche described the ideal future human as the overman, called by what German term?
Which book features a prophet who descends from a mountain after ten years of solitude?
What is the title of his 1872 book on Greek tragedy that contrasts the Apollonian and Dionysian?

q: Answer these questions about Hobbes's political thought.
parts: In Hobbes's thought, people live without any government in what condition?
Which book of 1651 argues that people should obey an absolute sovereign?
What term names the agreement by which people give up natural rights to a ruler, an idea shared by Locke and Rousseau?

q: Answer these questions about Rousseau's ideas.
parts: Which 1762 book argues that legitimate authority comes from an agreement among free people?
What term names the collective will of the people aimed at the common good?
Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality idealized a primitive human, often called what "savage"?

q: Answer these questions about Hegel's ideas.
parts: What term names Hegel's method of moving from thesis and antithesis to synthesis?
What German word for "spirit" or "mind" names the subject of his Phenomenology?
Hegel's philosophy of history states that history shows the unfolding of what abstract concept?

q: Answer these questions about Marx and Marxism.
parts: Who was Marx's lifelong collaborator and co-author of the Communist Manifesto?
Marx called which social class, who own the means of production, the ruling class under capitalism?
Marx's phrase "opium of the people" appears in his critique of which philosopher's Philosophy of Right?

q: Answer these questions about John Stuart Mill's works and ideas.
parts: Which work of 1859 defends freedom of speech and individuality?
What principle holds that power may be used against a person only to prevent harm to others?
Mill credited which wife, whom he married in 1851, with major influence on his work?

q: This Australian philosopher argued in "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" that if you could save a child drowning in a shallow pond at small cost to yourself, you ought to do so, and that distance should not matter. He wrote Animal Liberation, which criticized what he called speciesism. He teaches at Princeton and is associated with effective altruism. For 10 points, name this utilitarian ethicist.

This thinker's novel Nausea and play No Exit, which includes the line "Hell is other people," explore freedom. His major philosophical work, Being and Nothingness, describes the condition of denying one's own freedom as "bad faith." He declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature. For 10 points, name this French existentialist and partner of Simone de Beauvoir.

This French philosopher wrote The Second Sex, which includes the line "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." She also wrote The Ethics of Ambiguity and the novel The Mandarins. She was the long-time partner of Jean-Paul Sartre. For 10 points, name this feminist existentialist.

This Algerian-born French writer used the myth of a man condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever to illustrate the absurd condition. He wrote the novels The Stranger and The Plague and won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature. He famously wrote, "One must imagine Sisyphus happy." For 10 points, name this author of The Myth of Sisyphus.

In this thought experiment, parties choose the principles of a just society without knowing their own race, class, talents, or religion. It forms part of the "original position" in A Theory of Justice. John Rawls argued that people behind it would choose principles that protect the worst-off. For 10 points, name this device named for a covering that blocks sight of one's own social position.

In this thought experiment by John Searle, a man who does not know Chinese sits in a room manipulating symbols according to a rule book and passes out answers in Chinese. Searle used it to argue that running a program cannot by itself produce understanding. It is directed against "strong AI." For 10 points, name this thought experiment, named for a room.

Alan Turing proposed this test in the 1950 paper "Computing Machinery and Intelligence." A human judge converses by text with a hidden person and a hidden machine, and the machine passes if the judge cannot reliably tell them apart. Turing originally called it the "imitation game." For 10 points, name this test of machine intelligence.

This Dominican friar of the thirteenth century wrote the Summa Theologica, which contains the "Five Ways," arguments for God's existence. He united Christian doctrine with the philosophy of Aristotle and is called the "Angelic Doctor." He was born in Aquino. For 10 points, name this medieval Italian scholastic.

This bishop of Hippo wrote that he had been drawn to Manichaeism before being converted in Milan, where he heard sermons of Ambrose. His mother, Monica, prayed for his conversion. He developed the doctrine of original sin in debates with Pelagius. For 10 points, name this North African church father who wrote after the sack of Rome in 410.

This medieval rabbi, born in Cordoba, wrote the Guide for the Perplexed, which tries to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with Jewish law. He also compiled the fourteen-volume law code Mishneh Torah and a list of thirteen principles of faith. He served as physician at the court in Cairo. For 10 points, name this scholar also known as the Rambam.

This Andalusian philosopher, called "the Commentator" in the Latin West, wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle. He replied to al-Ghazali in The Incoherence of the Incoherence. He served as a judge in Seville and Cordoba. For 10 points, name this Muslim philosopher also known as Ibn Rushd.

This Persian philosopher was born near Bukhara and wrote the Book of Healing and the Canon of Medicine. He imagined a "floating man" who is suspended in the air and deprived of all sensation but still aware of himself. He argued that God is the "necessary existent." For 10 points, name this Islamic polymath also called Ibn Sina.

This man studied law in London and worked as a lawyer in South Africa, where he founded Tolstoy Farm. Back in India, he promoted homespun cloth called khadi and launched the Quit India movement in 1942. He was killed by Nathuram Godse in 1948. For 10 points, name this leader of Indian independence, who was called "Mahatma."

This text is part of the epic Mahabharata and takes the form of a dialogue on a battlefield at Kurukshetra. Arjuna hesitates to fight his kinsmen, and his charioteer Krishna teaches him about duty and detachment from the fruits of action. It presents several paths, including karma yoga and bhakti. For 10 points, name this Hindu scripture whose title means "Song of the Lord."

These ancient Indian texts, which conclude the Vedas, contain the phrase "tat tvam asi," or "you are that." They teach that the individual self is identical to the ultimate reality of the universe. Arthur Schopenhauer called them the solace of his life. For 10 points, name these philosophical texts, the basis of Vedanta.

In this game-theory scenario, two arrested suspects are separately offered a deal for betraying each other. Each does better by betraying no matter what the other does, yet both are worse off than if both had stayed silent. Albert Tucker named it. For 10 points, name this game theory scenario about cooperation and defection.

Garrett Hardin popularized this idea in a 1968 essay in Science. It describes how individuals acting in their own interest can deplete a shared resource, such as a pasture in which each herder adds more animals. An earlier 1833 pamphlet by William Forster Lloyd used the example of cattle grazing. For 10 points, name this concept in ethics and economics.

Cicero, Thomas Aquinas, and John Locke are major figures in this tradition. It claims that certain moral principles are built into human nature or reason and are universal. Martin Luther King Jr. invoked it when he argued that an unjust law is no law at all. For 10 points, name this theory that law should reflect universal moral truths.

Charles Sanders Peirce, William James, and John Dewey were founders of this American school of thought. It judges ideas by their practical effects and consequences. James described the truth of an idea as its "cash value." For 10 points, name this philosophy that emphasizes practical results.

This Russian-born novelist wrote Atlas Shrugged and The Fountainhead. She promoted a philosophy called Objectivism, which champions reason, individualism, and laissez-faire capitalism. Her essays collected in The Virtue of Selfishness defend egoism. For 10 points, name this author born Alisa Rosenbaum.

One version of this paradox says: "This sentence is false." If the sentence is true, then it is false, but if it is false, then it is true. Tradition ties it to Epimenides the Cretan, who said that all Cretans are liars. Alfred Tarski's work on truth was in part a response to it. For 10 points, name this paradox of self-reference.

Eubulides of Miletus is credited with this paradox, whose name comes from the Greek word for "heap." One grain of wheat is not a heap, and adding one grain never turns a non-heap into a heap, yet a large pile of grains is a heap. It is the standard example of the problem of vagueness. For 10 points, name this paradox.

This thought experiment describes a donkey placed exactly halfway between two identical bales of hay. Unable to choose, it starves. It is named for a fourteenth-century French priest and is used in debates about free will and rational choice. For 10 points, name this paradox about a hungry animal.

Robert Nozick presented this thought experiment in Anarchy, State, and Utopia. You are offered a chance to plug into a machine that would give you any experiences you desire, all indistinguishable from reality. Most people refuse, which Nozick took as evidence against hedonism. For 10 points, name this thought experiment.

This political philosophy opposes all forms of compulsory government and hierarchy. Its thinkers include Emma Goldman and Mikhail Bakunin, and its symbol is a circled A. Its Spanish version was prominent in the CNT during the 1930s. For 10 points, name this movement that advocates a stateless society.

This group of philosophers and scientists met in a city on the Danube in the 1920s and 1930s. Moritz Schlick led it, and Rudolf Carnap and Otto Neurath were members. They defended the principle that a statement has meaning only if it can be verified. For 10 points, name this group of logical positivists in Austria's capital.

In this thought experiment by Frank Jackson, a scientist raised in a black-and-white room knows every physical fact about the neurophysiology of color vision. When she steps out and sees a red tomato, she seems to learn something new. Jackson used it to argue against physicalism. For 10 points, name this thought experiment about a color scientist named for a woman.

This view holds that the right action is the one that best promotes the agent's own interests. It differs from psychological egoism, which claims that people in fact only act from self-interest. Thomas Hobbes is often read as a psychological egoist. For 10 points, name this ethical theory, in contrast with altruism.

This second-century Indian Buddhist founded the Madhyamaka, or Middle Way school. His Mulamadhyamakakarika argues that all phenomena are empty of inherent existence. He is considered a central figure of Mahayana. For 10 points, name this philosopher who developed the doctrine of sunyata, or emptiness.

David Chalmers popularized this thought experiment of a being that is physically identical to a normal person and acts the same, but has no inner conscious experience. He argues that if such a being is conceivable, physicalism is false. For 10 points, name this undead-themed philosophical being.
Answer these questions about Augustine's works.
parts: Which autobiographical work of about 400 describes his youth and conversion?
Which book, written after the sack of Rome in 410, contrasts an earthly and a heavenly society?
Augustine served as bishop of the city of Hippo, in the Roman province of what continent's north?

q: Answer these questions about Thomas Aquinas.
parts: Which Greek philosopher was called "the Philosopher" by Aquinas?
What term names Aquinas's five arguments for God, such as the argument from motion?
Aquinas taught at the university of which French city?

q: Answer these questions about existentialist writers' works.
parts: Which 1943 book by Jean-Paul Sartre argues that humans are condemned to be free?
Which 1949 book by Simone de Beauvoir analyzes the social construction of womanhood?
Which Camus novel of 1942 is narrated by Meursault, who is condemned for killing a man on an Algerian beach?

q: Answer these questions about Gandhi's campaigns.
parts: What Indian term, meaning "truth-force," names Gandhi's method of nonviolent resistance?
What 1930 march led Gandhi to the sea to protest the British tax on a basic commodity?
What is the title of Gandhi's autobiography, which describes experiments with truth?

q: Answer these questions about rules of logic.
parts: Which Latin-named rule says that if P implies Q and P is true, then Q is true?
Which rule says that if P implies Q and Q is false, then P is false?
What Latin phrase names a proof that assumes a claim and derives an absurdity?

q: Answer these questions about anarchist thinkers.
parts: Which French thinker wrote What Is Property?, which says that "property is theft"?
Which Russian prince wrote Mutual Aid, arguing that cooperation is a factor in evolution?
Which Russian anarchist quarreled with Karl Marx in the First International?

q: Answer these questions about schools of Buddhism.
parts: Which school of Buddhism, whose name means "teaching of the elders," is dominant in Sri Lanka and Thailand?
Which major branch, whose name means "great vehicle," is followed in China, Japan, and Korea?
Which tantric branch, whose name means "thunderbolt vehicle," is associated with Tibet?

q: Answer these questions about philosophy of mind.
parts: What term names the puzzle of why physical processes give rise to subjective experience, identified by David Chalmers?
What Latin plural term names the subjective qualities of experience, such as the redness of red?
What theory holds that mental states are defined by their causal roles rather than by what they are made of?

q: This man's first revelation is said to have come in a cave on Jabal al-Nour called Hira, where he often meditated. His early followers were persecuted by the Quraysh, and he lost his wife Khadijah and his uncle Abu Talib in the same "year of sorrow." In 622 he migrated to Yathrib, and he later returned to conquer his birthplace almost without bloodshed. For 10 points, name this final prophet of Islam, who received the Quran.

This city's Sacred Mosque contains a cube-shaped building toward which Muslims face when praying. It was the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad, and non-Muslims are forbidden to enter it. Pilgrims travel there during the Hajj each year. For 10 points, name this holy city in Saudi Arabia.

In 622 the Prophet Muhammad made a journey known as the Hijra to this city, then called Yathrib, after persecution in his hometown. His tomb lies beneath the green dome of the Prophet's Mosque here. The Constitution named for this city set up an agreement among its tribes. For 10 points, name this holy city of Islam in Saudi Arabia, second only to Mecca.

This holy month of the Islamic calendar involves fasting from dawn until sunset each day. It is the month in which the Quran was first revealed, and it ends with the festival of Eid al-Fitr. Muslims often break the fast with a meal called iftar. For 10 points, name this ninth month.

Pilgrims taking part in this event wear plain white garments called ihram and circle the Kaaba seven times. Other rites include running between the hills of Safa and Marwa and standing on the plain of Arafat. Every able Muslim who can afford it should do this at least once. For 10 points, name this annual pilgrimage to Mecca, one of the five pillars of Islam.

According to Muslim tradition, this cube-shaped structure was rebuilt by Ibrahim and his son Ismail. It is draped in a black cloth called the kiswah and holds the Black Stone in one corner. Muslims around the world face it during prayer. For 10 points, name this shrine at the center of the Sacred Mosque in Mecca.

Verses of this text are read in the original Arabic during daily prayers and memorized by people called hafiz. Its chapters are arranged roughly from longest to shortest, apart from the short opening one. The Uthmanic edition is the basis of every modern copy. For 10 points, name this scripture.

This event of 622 is the starting point of the Islamic calendar. Muhammad's cousin Ali is said to have slept in his bed to deceive pursuers while he left Mecca with Abu Bakr and hid in a cave. The travelers' destination was Yathrib. For 10 points, name this emigration of Muhammad and his followers to Medina.

A disputed succession after Muhammad's death in 632 split Islam into two major branches. The larger branch, which makes up roughly eighty-five to ninety percent of Muslims, accepted Abu Bakr as the first caliph. Its name refers to following the tradition of the Prophet. For 10 points, name this branch of Islam, contrasted with Shia.

This branch of Islam holds that leadership should have passed to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law. Its followers commemorate the martyrdom of Husayn, and most of them live in Iran, Iraq, and Azerbaijan. They honor leaders called imams. For 10 points, name this second-largest branch of Islam.

This woman was the wife of Ali and the mother of Hasan and Husayn. She is sometimes given the title al-Zahra, "the radiant." Both Sunnis and Shia revere her, and one of the most successful Fatimid dynasties took her name. For 10 points, name this youngest daughter of Muhammad and Khadijah.

This man was Muhammad's close friend and father of his wife Aisha. After the Prophet's death he became the first of the Rashidun, or "rightly guided," caliphs. His short reign saw the Ridda Wars against tribes that broke away. For 10 points, name this first caliph, whose surname means "father of the virgin."

This caliph, the second of the Rashidun, ruled from 634 to 644 and oversaw conquests of Syria, Egypt, and Persia. He is credited with starting the Hijri calendar and with entering Jerusalem peacefully. He was assassinated by a Persian slave named Abu Lulu. For 10 points, name this successor of Abu Bakr.

This third caliph oversaw the compilation of a standard written version of the Quran. He belonged to the Umayyad clan and was married to two of Muhammad's daughters in turn. His murder in 656 led to the First Fitna, or civil war. For 10 points, name this Rashidun caliph, successor to Umar.

This man was Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and he became the fourth caliph in 656. His supporters, the party of this man, gave the Shia branch its name. He moved the capital to Kufa and was killed there in 661. For 10 points, name this figure who is regarded as the first imam by Shia Muslims.

This title belonged to the political and religious successors of Muhammad, such as Abu Bakr and Umar. Later holders ruled from Damascus, Baghdad, Cairo, and Istanbul. The institution ended in 1924 when it was abolished by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk. For 10 points, give this title of the leader of the Muslim community.

These collections record the sayings and actions of Muhammad as reported by his companions. Compilers such as Bukhari and Muslim judged the chain of narrators for each one. Together with the Quran they are a key source of Islamic law. For 10 points, name these reports of the Prophet's words and deeds.

This term, meaning "the path to the water source," refers to Islamic religious law. It is derived from the Quran, hadith, consensus, and analogy, and it is interpreted by scholars called muftis. Four Sunni schools, including the Hanafi and Maliki, apply it. For 10 points, give this term for Islamic law.

This pillar of Islam requires Muslims to give a fixed portion of their savings, usually two and a half percent, to the needy. Its name means "purification." It is separate from voluntary charity called sadaqah. For 10 points, name this obligatory almsgiving.

Muslims perform this ritual five times a day facing Mecca, after performing ablution called wudu. It involves bowing and prostrating on a mat. The call to it is given by the muezzin. For 10 points, name this Islamic prayer, the second pillar of Islam.

The first pillar of Islam is a statement of faith beginning "There is no god but God." It adds that Muhammad is the messenger of God. Saying it with sincere belief makes a person a Muslim. For 10 points, name this declaration of faith.

This festival marks the end of Ramadan and is celebrated for three days. Muslims dress in new clothes, attend special prayers, and give a charity called zakat al-fitr. Sweets are exchanged among families. For 10 points, name this festival whose name means "breaking of the fast."

This festival honors Ibrahim's willingness to sacrifice his son at God's command. It falls on the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah, at the end of the Hajj, and families sacrifice a sheep or goat and share the meat. It is also called the "Greater Eid." For 10 points, name this festival of sacrifice.

On this night near the end of Ramadan, according to tradition, the first verses of the Quran were sent down to Muhammad. The Quran says it is better than a thousand months. Muslims often seek it on odd-numbered nights of the last ten days. For 10 points, name this "Night of Power."

Muslims worship in this kind of building, which often has a dome and a tall tower. Worshippers remove their shoes before entering the prayer hall. The Great Umayyad building in Damascus and the Blue one in Istanbul are famous examples. For 10 points, give this Islamic house of worship.

The muezzin traditionally gives the call to prayer from this feature of a mosque. These tall, slender towers are found at the Great Mosque of Samarra, which has a spiral one called the Malwiya. Many mosques have four or more. For 10 points, name this tower.

This feature of a mosque is a niche in the wall that indicates the direction of Mecca. It is often decorated with tile or calligraphy, and the imam stands in front of it to lead prayers. A nearby stepped pulpit is called a minbar. For 10 points, name this niche.

According to Islamic belief, this angel revealed the Quran to Muhammad. He is called Jibril in Arabic and is also said to have accompanied the Prophet on the Night Journey. Christians know the same angel as the one who announced Jesus's birth to Mary. For 10 points, name this archangel.

This shrine in Jerusalem is topped by a golden dome and stands over the rock from which Muhammad is said to have ascended to heaven. It was built by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik around 691. It stands on the Temple Mount. For 10 points, name this Islamic shrine.

Practitioners of this mystical branch of Islam seek direct experience of God. Some orders use music, such as the Mawlawi order, whose members whirl in a ceremony called sama. Rumi is its best-known poet. For 10 points, name this tradition whose members are sometimes called dervishes.

The first dynasty of Muslim caliphs, founded by Muawiya in 661, ruled from Damascus. Its rule eventually reached Spain and the Indus. It was overthrown by the Abbasids in 750. For 10 points, name this dynasty, whose name comes from a clan of the Quraysh.

This dynasty built a capital called the "Round City" at Baghdad in 762 under al-Mansur. Its rule produced a "House of Wisdom" that translated Greek works during the reign of al-Mamun. Hulagu Khan ended its power in 1258. For 10 points, name this caliphal dynasty that replaced the Umayyads.

In 680 Husayn, grandson of Muhammad, was killed in this Iraqi city by the army of Yazid. Shia Muslims mourn his death on the day of Ashura, and pilgrims visit his shrine here. For 10 points, name this city, the site of the most important Shia martyrdom.
Answer these questions about the Hajj.
parts: Pilgrims on the Hajj travel to which holy city in Saudi Arabia?
Pilgrims gather on a plain outside the city on the ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah for the "Standing" ritual. Name this plain or mountain.
The well said to have gushed for Hagar and her son Ismail lies near the Kaaba. Name it.

q: This man was born a prince in Lumbini, in present-day Nepal, and left his palace after seeing an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and an ascetic. He fasted for years before accepting a bowl of rice milk from a girl named Sujata. After meditating under a fig tree, he taught his first sermon at the Deer Park in Sarnath. For 10 points, name this founder of Buddhism.

Buddhism teaches that suffering exists, that it has a cause in craving, that it can end, and that a path leads to its end. The Buddha gave these in his first sermon after enlightenment. For 10 points, name this set of four central teachings.

This path consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. It is the fourth of the Four Noble Truths. It is called the Middle Way between luxury and extreme asceticism. For 10 points, name this Buddhist path to the end of suffering.

Buddhists seek this state of liberation, whose name literally means "blowing out," in which the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion are extinguished. Reaching it ends the cycle of rebirth. The Pali form of this word is nibbana. For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhist practice.

The Buddha attained enlightenment while meditating beneath this kind of tree at Bodh Gaya. It is a species of fig, and descendants of the original are venerated in Sri Lanka and India. Buddhist pilgrims visit the site. For 10 points, name this tree, whose name means "awakening."

This branch of Buddhism, whose name means "School of the Elders," is dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, and Myanmar. It follows the Pali Canon and emphasizes the ideal of the arhat. For 10 points, name this branch, often contrasted with Mahayana.

This branch of Buddhism, whose name means "Great Vehicle," spread to China, Korea, and Japan. It emphasizes the ideal of the bodhisattva, who delays nirvana to help others. Pure Land and Zen belong to it. For 10 points, name this branch of Buddhism.

This school of Mahayana Buddhism, called Chan in China, emphasizes seated meditation known as zazen. It was brought to Japan by Eisai and Dogen, and its masters use riddles called koans. For 10 points, name this Japanese form of Buddhism.

This title is held by the spiritual leader of the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, who is believed to be a reincarnation of his predecessor. The current holder fled Tibet in 1959 and settled in Dharamsala. For 10 points, give this title of the most famous Tibetan Buddhist leader.

This Tibetan school of Buddhism, whose name means "Diamond Vehicle," uses mantras, mandalas, and ritual practices. It arrived with Padmasambhava and Atisha. For 10 points, name this form of Buddhism practiced in Tibet and Bhutan, also called Tantric Buddhism.

This religion is practiced by roughly a billion people, mainly in India and Nepal. It has no single founder or scripture, but its texts include the Vedas and Upanishads. For 10 points, name this religion whose major gods include Vishnu and Shiva.

These oldest scriptures of Hinduism are written in Sanskrit and are divided into four collections, including the Rigveda. They contain hymns to deities such as Agni and Indra. For 10 points, name these sacred texts, from which the Upanishads emerged.

These philosophical texts end the Vedas and are called Vedanta, "the end of the Veda." They discuss the identity of atman and Brahman. Over 100 exist, and ten principal ones were commented on by Shankara. For 10 points, name these texts.

This text is a conversation set on the battlefield of Kurukshetra between a warrior and his charioteer. The warrior is Arjuna, who hesitates to fight his kin. It is part of the Mahabharata. For 10 points, name this "Song of God," a central Hindu scripture.

In Hinduism, this god is the creator in a trinity with Vishnu and Shiva. He is depicted with four faces and is often shown with a swan. For 10 points, name this god, not to be confused with the impersonal ultimate reality called Brahman.

This Hindu god preserves the universe and descends to earth in forms called avatars. His ten main incarnations include Rama and Krishna. He sleeps on the serpent Shesha. For 10 points, name this member of the Trimurti.

This Hindu god is depicted with a third eye, a trident, and the Ganges flowing from his hair. He is both destroyer and ascetic, and is worshipped in the form of the lingam. His wife is Parvati. For 10 points, name this member of the Trimurti.

This elephant-headed Hindu god is the remover of obstacles and the son of Shiva and Parvati. He is invoked at the start of ventures and rides a mouse. For 10 points, name this god, whose festival Ganesh Chaturthi is celebrated every year.

This Hindu god grew up among cowherds in Vrindavan, where he played the flute and danced with the gopis. He later killed his uncle Kamsa and founded the city of Dwarka. His charioteering for Arjuna is told in a famous scripture. For 10 points, name this eighth avatar of Vishnu.

This Hindu epic tells of a prince's fourteen-year exile, the abduction of his wife by a ten-headed king, and the aid of a monkey god in a battle at Lanka. It is attributed to the sage Valmiki, who is called the first poet. Dussehra honors its hero's victory. For 10 points, name this Sanskrit epic.

In this epic, Yudhishthira loses his kingdom in a game of dice to Duryodhana's side, and the five brothers are exiled for thirteen years. Bhishma lies on a bed of arrows, and Karna is killed when his chariot wheel sticks in the mud. A dog follows the victors to heaven at the end. For 10 points, name this Sanskrit epic attributed to Vyasa.

This festival of lights, celebrated in October or November, honors Lakshmi and Rama's return to Ayodhya. Families light clay lamps called diyas and set off fireworks. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival.
This spring festival of colors involves throwing colored powder and water. It celebrates the burning of Holika and Krishna's love for Radha. For 10 points, name this Hindu festival.

In Hindu and Buddhist thought, this concept holds that a person's actions have consequences that shape future lives. Good deeds produce good outcomes and bad deeds the opposite. For 10 points, name this principle of cause and effect.

In Hinduism, liberation from the cycle of birth and death is called this. It is the final goal of life, reached by realizing the unity of the self and Brahman. Jains and Buddhists call a similar state nirvana. For 10 points, give this Sanskrit term.

Hindus consider this river sacred and bathe in it at cities such as Varanasi and Haridwar. The goddess of the same name is said to have descended from heaven through Shiva's hair. For 10 points, name this river of northern India.
This religion was founded by Guru Nanak in the Punjab in the fifteenth century. Its scripture is the Guru Granth Sahib, and followers wear the five Ks. For 10 points, name this monotheistic religion.

This Chinese philosopher compiled maxims on filial piety, ritual, and the gentleman, which were collected in the Analects. He lived in the Spring and Autumn period, and his followers included Mencius. For 10 points, name this founder of Confucianism.

The Tao Te Ching is attributed to this legendary sage, said to have written it before leaving China on a water buffalo. For 10 points, name this figure traditionally regarded as the founder of Daoism.

This Japanese religion has no founder and venerates spirits called kami. Its shrines are marked by gateways called torii, and its priests perform purification rituals. For 10 points, name this indigenous religion of Japan.

This Indian religion's twenty-fourth tirthankara was Mahavira, who taught strict nonviolence. Its monks may wear white robes or go naked, and some sweep the ground before them to avoid harming insects. For 10 points, name this religion.

q: This religion's holy book, the Avesta, includes hymns called the Gathas. Its priests tend fires in temples, and it holds that the universe is a battle between good and evil. Its followers in India are known as Parsis. For 10 points, name this ancient Persian religion that worships Ahura Mazda.

This prophet is said to have received a vision of Ahura Mazda at about age thirty. He composed the Gathas and taught the dualism of truth and the lie. He is believed to have lived in ancient Iran. For 10 points, name this founder of a religion also called Mazdaism.

In Zoroastrian belief, this evil spirit, also called Ahriman, opposes creation through lies, disease, and death. Its name means "destructive spirit," and it is contrasted with Spenta Mainyu. At the end of time the Saoshyant is expected to defeat it. For 10 points, give this adversary of Ahura Mazda.

This man claimed that the angel Moroni led him to golden plates buried in a hill in upstate New York. He translated them as a scripture and founded a church in 1830. He was killed by a mob in Carthage, Illinois, in 1844. For 10 points, name this founder of the Latter-day Saint movement.

This scripture is divided into books named for figures such as Nephi, Alma, and Ether. Followers of the Latter-day Saint movement believe it was translated from golden plates. It describes Jesus visiting the Americas. For 10 points, name this scripture first published in 1830.

After Joseph Smith's death, this man led the Mormon pioneers west to the Great Salt Lake in 1847. He became the second president of the church and the first governor of Utah Territory. He had many wives. For 10 points, name this leader.

This city in Utah was founded by Mormon pioneers in 1847 and is the headquarters of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Temple Square is its center. For 10 points, name this state capital.

This religion was founded in nineteenth-century Persia and teaches the unity of God, religion, and humanity. Its Lotus Temple is in Delhi, and its holiest shrines are in Haifa and Acre. For 10 points, name this faith, founded by Baha'u'llah.

This Persian nobleman, born Mirza Husayn-Ali, declared himself a manifestation of God in 1863. He was exiled to Acre and wrote the Kitab-i-Aqdas. For 10 points, name this founder of the Baha'i Faith, whose name means "Glory of God."

This religion began in Jamaica in the 1930s and regards Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia as divine. Many followers wear dreadlocks and avoid meat, and the use of cannabis is a sacrament. For 10 points, name this movement associated with Bob Marley.

This religion, which blends West African Yoruba beliefs with Catholic saints, developed among enslaved people in Cuba. Practitioners honor spirits called orishas. For 10 points, name this religion, also known as Regla de Ocha.

This Afro-Caribbean religion was developed in Haiti and honors spirits called lwa. Its priests are called houngans and its priestesses mambos. For 10 points, name this religion, often misrepresented in films.

These priests of the ancient Celts served as judges, teachers, and religious leaders. Julius Caesar describes their sacrifices, and Roman sources say they venerated mistletoe and oak. For 10 points, name these ancient Celtic priests.

This Quaker movement founder wrote a journal and preached that the Inner Light of God is in each person. Born in Leicestershire in 1624, he was repeatedly imprisoned. For 10 points, name this founder of the Religious Society of Friends.

This Christian group, living mostly in Pennsylvania and Ohio, avoids modern technology and drives horse-drawn buggies. They follow an Anabaptist tradition named for a Swiss leader, Jakob Ammann. For 10 points, name this group.

This Christian denomination, founded after the Great Disappointment of 1844, observes Saturday as the Sabbath. It emphasizes health and was shaped by Ellen G. White. For 10 points, name this denomination, which runs Loma Linda University.

This denomination was named by Charles Taze Russell's followers and publishes The Watchtower. Members go door to door, refuse blood transfusions, and do not celebrate birthdays. For 10 points, name this group.

This Christian denomination was founded by Mary Baker Eddy, who wrote Science and Health. It teaches that illness is an illusion that prayer can heal, and it publishes a daily newspaper in Boston. For 10 points, name this church.

This tradition emphasizes the experience of the Holy Spirit, including speaking in tongues. It grew from the 1906 Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles and is now one of the fastest-growing Christian movements. For 10 points, name this movement.

This prophet, born in Persia in the third century, taught a dualistic religion that blended Christian, Zoroastrian, and Buddhist elements. His religion spread from Rome to China before dying out. For 10 points, name this founder of Manichaeism.

This mystery religion of the Roman army worshipped a god who slew a sacred bull. Its followers met in underground temples called mithraea. For 10 points, name this religion, named for a god of Persian origin.

This religious group in northern Iraq venerates Melek Taus, the Peacock Angel, and prays facing the sun. Their holiest site is the valley shrine of Lalish. They are mostly Kurdish-speaking and have suffered massacres in 2014. Membership is traditionally limited to those born into it. For 10 points, name this religion.

This theological system of the Hellenistic era taught that the material world was created by a lesser being and that salvation comes through secret knowledge. The Nag Hammadi library contained its texts. For 10 points, name this movement, whose name comes from the Greek for "knowledge."

This monument in Wiltshire, England, is a ring of large standing stones. Some think it was used for astronomical purposes, and people gather there at the summer solstice. For 10 points, name this prehistoric monument.

This 1890 movement among Plains tribes, started by the Paiute prophet Wovoka, promised the return of the dead and the end of white expansion. Dancers wore shirts believed to be bulletproof. It was suppressed at Wounded Knee. For 10 points, name this ritual.

This Ethiopian emperor, born Tafari Makonnen, is revered as the returned Messiah by Rastafari. He ruled from 1930 until he was deposed in 1974, with a break during the Italian occupation. He addressed the League of Nations in 1936 after Mussolini's invasion, and he gave Jamaica's Rastas their name for him. For 10 points, name this man.

This word describes the belief that natural objects, such as rivers, rocks, and trees, have a spirit. Edward Tylor used it in the nineteenth century to describe early religion. For 10 points, give this term.

This religious figure, in many Siberian and Native cultures, enters trances to communicate with spirits and heal. The word comes from the Tungus language. For 10 points, name this kind of practitioner.

This Unitarian principle, found in Enlightenment Europe, holds that God created the universe but does not intervene in it. Thomas Jefferson and Benjamin Franklin held views of this sort. For 10 points, name this belief.

This nickname is commonly applied to members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, after a prophet-historian in their scripture. Members avoid coffee and alcohol and often serve two-year missions. For 10 points, give this nickname.

parts: Which founder said he received the Book of Mormon from an angel?
What angel did he say showed him the golden plates?
